[7] (about=Jerome, episodic, t12 @2026-07-10T20:11:00) that is exactly what the Ha-RGB blend does. you keep the full broadband RGB as your colour base and add the Ha emission only where it contributes signal. the PixInsight workflow I use is: LinearFit both datasets to match background levels, then use PixelMath with the expression: Ha_weight multiplied by Ha plus open-bracket 1 minus Ha_weight close-bracket multiplied by R, where Ha_weight is typically 0.7. you replace the red channel with this blended value and recombine. the result is your broadband warmth with Ha emission boosting the ionised hydrogen regions. it is the best of both methods technically speaking. try it on the Orion core and tell me if the Trapezium halo structure changes.
[8] (about=Jerome, episodic, t12 @2026-07-10T20:07:00) the Ha-RGB blend is not complicated once you understand what you are doing, but there are three things most people get wrong that kill the result. first: your Ha data needs to be calibrated and stacked separately, not mixed in during the initial integration. second: in PixInsight you use the ChannelCombination process with Ha mapped to the red channel of a synthetic luminance, then combine with a Luminance mask to protect star colours. third, and this is where most broadband imagers fail: you need to apply a Hue-Saturation adjustment after the blend to desaturate the magenta cast that appears in the red-blue transition zones around HII regions. if you skip that step your stars look radioactive and the nebula looks like a bad Instagram filter. send me your Orion FITS stack and I will step through it with you here in the chat.
[9] (about=Jerome, episodic, t6 @2026-04-03T20:22:00) send me the FITS file. the issue is almost certainly your background extraction in PixInsight. if you are using automatic background extractor before separating the channels you will get that muddy look. I will walk you through the correct sequence. it will take 20 minutes.
